procedural_history.originating_court: Additional Sessions Judge, Shajapur, Madhya Pradesh
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 06.12.2006 of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh, Bench at Indore in Criminal Appeal No. 1370 of 2001.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Indore in Criminal Appeal No. 1370 of 2001 set aside the conviction of the respondents (except respondent No. 1) under Sections 302/149 and 325/129 IPC. Respondent No. 1 was held guilty under Section 304 (Part-I) IPC and sentenced to ten years R.I. and a fine.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, Kalpana K. Tripathy, approached the Supreme Court by way of a special leave petition challenging the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in acquitting accused Nos. 2 to 9, given the presence of an injured eye-witness and a dying declaration.

facts: Nine accused were prosecuted for an assault on two brothers, PW-1 (Dinesh) and the deceased (Rajesh), following a dispute over cattle grazing.
Accused No. 1 was armed with a gun, while the others were allegedly armed with lathis and swords.
The deceased died from a single gunshot wound to the thigh, inflicted by Accused No. 1.
The eye-witness, PW-1, sustained four injuries from a hard and blunt object.
The prosecution's case relied on the testimony of the injured eye-witness (PW-1) and a dying declaration made by the deceased.
The High Court acquitted accused Nos. 2 to 9 but convicted Accused No. 1 for a lesser offence.
law: For a conviction to be sustained, testimonial evidence, such as that from an eye-witness or a dying declaration, should be corroborated by other evidence, particularly medical evidence.
When there is a significant contradiction between the testimony of witnesses and the objective medical evidence, the testimony can be deemed unreliable.
General and omnibus allegations against multiple accused persons without specific corroboration are insufficient to fix individual liability.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the two key pieces of evidence against accused Nos. 2 to 9: the eye-witness testimony and the dying declaration.

Regarding the eye-witness (PW-1), the Court noted that his statement was a "general and omnibus" claim that all accused assaulted both him and the deceased. This was contradicted by the medical evidence.
The deceased had only one injury (the gunshot wound from Accused No. 1) and no injuries from lathis or sharp weapons, which belied PW-1's claim that others also assaulted him.
PW-1 himself had only four blunt-force injuries, making it difficult to believe he was attacked by eight people and impossible to determine who caused which injury.

Regarding the dying declaration, the Court found it to be contradictory and uncorroborated. The deceased first stated he only knew Accused No. 1 assaulted him, but then claimed Accused Nos. 2 and 3 hit him with a lathi.
This claim was directly contradicted by the medical evidence, as the deceased "did not suffer even a single scratch on his body except fire arm injury."

Since both the eye-witness account and the dying declaration were fundamentally inconsistent with the medical findings regarding the involvement of accused Nos. 2 to 9, the Court found the evidence against them to be unreliable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal and upheld the High Court's acquittal of accused Nos. 2 to 9 because the primary evidence against them—the testimony of the injured eye-witness and the dying declaration—was not credible as it was directly contradicted and belied by the objective medical evidence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court correctly altered the conviction of accused No. 1 from murder under Section 302 to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 (Part I).

facts: Accused No. 1 shot the deceased with a firearm.
The medical evidence showed that the entry wound was on the back of the deceased's left thigh.
The High Court had altered the trial court's conviction of accused No. 1 from murder under Section 302 to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 (Part I).
law: The distinction between murder (Section 302) and culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Section 304, Part I) depends on the accused's intention.
An intention to commit murder is typically inferred when an injury is inflicted on a vital part of the body, such as the upper limbs or above the waist.
application: The Supreme Court examined the medical evidence and noted the location of the gunshot wound on the back of the deceased's thigh.
The Court inferred from the location of the injury that if accused No. 1 had intended to kill the deceased, he would have aimed at a more vital part of the body.
By shooting the deceased in the thigh, the accused demonstrated an intention to cause a bodily injury likely to cause death, rather than a direct intention to commit murder.
This specific act and intention align with the definition of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 (Part I) of the IPC.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found "no infirmity" in the High Court's judgment, concluding that the High Court was justified in altering the conviction of accused No. 1 from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder based on the medical evidence, which did not support an intention to kill.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in acquitting accused Nos. 2 to 9, given the presence of an injured eye-witness and a dying declaration.
appellant_arguments: The High Court failed to appreciate that the nine accused were armed with weapons and came to the spot with a premeditated common intention to assault and kill the complainant and his brother.
Given the common intention, the High Court was not justified in setting aside the conviction of accused Nos. 2 to 9.
respondent_arguments: The general statement of the injured eyewitness (PW-1) about the participation of all accused is not corroborated by medical evidence.

The eyewitness (PW-1) claimed he was assaulted by all accused, but he only sustained four injuries from a hard and blunt object, with no injuries from a firearm or sharp-edged weapon, making it difficult to fix liability on specific individuals.

The dying declaration is contradictory, as the deceased first said he didn't know who assaulted him besides accused No. 1, but then named accused Nos. 2 and 3, a version which is also not corroborated by medical evidence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court correctly altered the conviction of accused No. 1 from murder under Section 302 to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 (Part I).
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in setting aside the conviction of accused No. 1 under Section 302 IPC (murder) and imposing a lesser punishment under Section 304 (Part I) IPC.
respondent_arguments: The medical evidence indicates that accused No. 1 did not have the intention to commit murder.
The act of accused No. 1 was to cause a bodily injury likely to cause death, which correctly falls under Section 304 (Part I) IPC, not Section 302 IPC.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An accused's intention to commit murder can be determined from medical evidence; where an injury is inflicted on a non-vital part of the body, it supports the inference that the act was to cause a bodily injury likely to cause death, rather than an intentional act of murder, thus warranting a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's judgment was justified because the evidence against accused Nos. 2 to 9, namely the eyewitness statement and the dying declaration, was not corroborated by medical evidence and was contradictory, making it impossible to fasten liability. Furthermore, the alteration of accused No. 1's conviction from murder to culpable homicide was correct, as the location of the gunshot wound on the deceased's thigh indicated an intention to cause a bodily injury likely to cause death, rather than a direct intention to kill.
legal_tests_applied: The principle that eyewitness testimony and dying declarations should be corroborated by medical evidence to be considered reliable, especially when assigning liability among multiple accused.

The distinction between murder under Section 302 IPC and culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 (Part I) IPC, which is determined by the accused's intention as inferred from the nature and location of the injury.
why_appellant_lost: The general statement of the injured eyewitness (PW-1) that he was assaulted by all accused persons was not corroborated by the medical evidence, as he sustained only four injuries from a hard and blunt object, with no injuries from a firearm or sharp-edged weapon.

The dying declaration of the deceased was contradictory; in the first declaration, he stated he did not know who assaulted him besides accused No. 1, while in the second, he named accused Nos. 2 and 3, a version also uncorroborated by medical evidence.

The medical evidence regarding accused No. 1's act did not support an intention to commit murder; if the intention was to kill with a firearm, the injury would likely have been on the upper limb or above the waist, not on the back of the left thigh.
why_respondent_won: The High Court correctly held that liability could not be fastened on accused Nos. 2 to 9 because the eyewitness testimony was general and uncorroborated, and the dying declaration was contradictory and also lacked medical corroboration.

The High Court correctly found that accused No. 1 was not having the intention to commit murder, but that his act was to cause a bodily injury which was likely to cause death, thus making him responsible for culpable homicide under Section 304 (Part I) IPC.
The location of the gunshot wound on the back of the deceased's left thigh supported the inference that the intention was not to kill, but to cause a lesser, though still fatal, injury.
